Hypothesis testing is often taught as a ritual:

```text
calculate p → compare with 0.05 → declare significance
```

That hides the real structure.

A test asks:

> **If a specified null model were true, how surprising would data like these be?**

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn
- Null and alternative hypotheses
- Test statistics and p-values
- Type I and Type II errors
- Statistical power
- Why statistical significance is not practical importance
:::

## The p-value

A p-value is the probability, **under the null model**, of observing a test statistic at least as incompatible with the null as the one observed.

It is **not** $P(H_0\mid\text{data})$.

## Interactive: move the observed z-statistic

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof zobs = Inputs.range([0,4], {value:1.96, step:.05, label:"|Observed z|"})
phi=z=>Math.exp(-z*z/2)/Math.sqrt(2*Math.PI)
grid=d3.range(-4.5,4.51,.02).map(x=>({x,y:phi(x),tail:Math.abs(x)>=zobs}))
cdf=x=>0.5*(1+((z)=>{const t=1/(1+.3275911*Math.abs(z)); const y=1-(((((1.061405429*t-1.453152027)*t)+1.421413741)*t-.284496736)*t+.254829592)*t*Math.exp(-z*z);return z>=0?y:-y;})(x/Math.SQRT2))
pval=2*(1-cdf(zobs))
html`<div class="ms-readout"><span>Two-sided p-value</span><b>${pval.toFixed(4)}</b></div>`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
 height:300,x:{label:"z"},y:{label:"Null density"},
 marks:[
  Plot.areaY(grid.filter(d=>d.tail),{x:"x",y:"y",fill:"#E11D48",fillOpacity:.25}),
  Plot.line(grid,{x:"x",y:"y",stroke:"#4F46E5",strokeWidth:2})
 ]
})
```

## Errors are defined across repeated decisions

| Reality | Do not reject $H_0$ | Reject $H_0$ |
|---|---|---|
| $H_0$ true | Correct | Type I error ($\alpha$) |
| $H_1$ true | Type II error ($\beta$) | Correct; power $=1-\beta$ |

## Animation: power rises with effect size and sample size

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
from scipy.stats import norm

rows=[]
alpha=.05
crit=norm.ppf(1-alpha/2)
for n in [20,50,100,200,500]:
    for d in np.linspace(0,0.6,61):
        mu=d*np.sqrt(n)
        power=norm.sf(crit-mu)+norm.cdf(-crit-mu)
        rows.append({"n":n,"effect":d,"power":power})
df=pd.DataFrame(rows)
fig=px.line(df,x="effect",y="power",animation_frame="n",range_y=[0,1],
            labels={"effect":"Standardized effect size","power":"Power"})
fig.add_hline(y=.8,line_dash="dash")
fig.update_layout(height=380)
fig.show()
```

## DS/ML Bridge

Hypothesis testing appears in:

- feature experiments,
- model comparison,
- uplift measurement,
- regression coefficient tests,
- monitoring shifts,
- controlled online experiments.

But with huge datasets, tiny effects can become statistically significant. Always pair inference with an **effect size** and domain relevance.

::: {.callout-warning}
## “Not significant” does not mean “no effect”
It can mean the study had too little information to distinguish the effect from noise.
:::

## Summary
- A p-value is computed assuming the null model.
- Type I error is a false positive; Type II error is a false negative.
- Power is the probability of detecting an effect under a specified alternative.
- Larger samples detect smaller effects.
- Statistical significance and practical importance are different questions.
